reading.rtitle: The Line That Gets Read Twice
paras: Somebody reads your file, and the honest number is about seven minutes. In those seven minutes the reader is not looking for a list. Every file already has a list: grades, a club, a season somewhere, a certificate. The list is what makes a file complete, and complete is not the same as memorable. What the reader is looking for is one line that says what is different about you now that was not different two years ago.

That is why the strongest files are written in two tenses and the weakest ones in one. A weak file only says what happened. I went, I played, I finished, I came back. It reads like a receipt. A strong file also says what has changed and has not stopped. I have played competitively since I was nine. I have not needed a translation for a year. I have kept the same routine since the season ended. A reader can do something with the second kind of sentence, because it points at today.

The word applicants use most is the one reviewers trust least, and that word is significant. Saying an experience was significant is not evidence; it is an adjective. What turns it into evidence is the consequence that came after it, written plainly and in the right tense. The advice reviewers give, when anybody asks them, is almost always the same and almost never followed. Cut half the adjectives, keep the dates, and make sure the reader can tell which parts of your file are finished and which parts are still going on.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, written for this lesson from the published guidance of international admissions offices

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A file should contain as long a list of achievements as the applicant can put together.
The reader has very little time, so what makes a file memorable is showing what has changed and is still true, not listing what happened.
Reviewers prefer files written only in the past simple, because a finished story is easier to follow.

listenings.text: I read about two thousand files a year, and on the first pass I give each one roughly seven minutes. People are shocked by that number, and they should not be. Seven minutes is enough, because after the first hundred you know exactly where the information is. What I want to say to a room full of counsellors is this. The files I remember are not the ones with the longest lists. Every file has a list. The files I remember tell me what has changed about the person, and that is a different sentence with a different tense in it. I went to Canada and I played in a league is a fact. I have not needed a translation since March is a person. And please, all of you, talk to your students about the word significant. They write that a experience was significant and they stop there, as if the adjective did the work. It does not. Show me what came after it. I can judge a consequence. I cannot judge an adjective, and after two thousand files I do not even read them any more.

The thing nobody tells you about the first month is that it is very easy to waste it. I wasted mine. There were four other Brazilians in my building and we did everything together, and it was comfortable, and my English did not move a centimetre in thirty days. What fixed it was not a course. I joined a student club where nobody spoke Portuguese, and I went twice a week even on the days I did not want to go. Since then a lot has changed, and the one I notice most is that I have stopped building sentences in my head before I open my mouth. I answer while I am still thinking, which sounds like a small thing and is not. About the certificate, because everybody asks me. I took mine before I applied and it opened the door, so I am not going to pretend it does not matter. But I tell people the same thing every time. The certificate proves the level, it does not build it, and those two things have to happen in that order or you just pay twice.
